nodes.label: Golitsyn
nodes.full: Prince Grigory Golitsyn, governor-general from 1896, applied the government's Russification policy against the Armenians, restricting their church schools, and in 1903 confiscating the property of the Armenian church; the measures were opposed by the Dashnaks, and an attempt was made on his life in October 1903; they were largely withdrawn in 1905 under his successor.
nodes.src: Ronald Suny, Looking toward Ararat (1993); Ronald Suny, The Making of the Georgian Nation (1994).

nodes.label: Vorontsov-Dashkov
nodes.full: Count Illarion Vorontsov-Dashkov, appointed viceroy in 1905 after the unrest, returned the Armenian church property, ended the policy of open Russification, allowed the use of local languages in schools and in the press, and worked to smooth over the nationalities' conflicts with the support of leading local figures.
nodes.src: Suny 1994; Audrey Altstadt, The Azerbaijani Turks (1992).

nodes.label: Special Transcaucasian Committee
nodes.full: After the abdication of the tsar in March 1917 the Provisional Government replaced the viceroyalty with a Special Transcaucasian Committee (Ozakom) of five members from the Duma, which governed in Tbilisi with soviets of soldiers and workers alongside, until the Bolshevik coup in Petrograd and the end of its authority in November.
nodes.src: Suny 1994; Richard Hovannisian, The Republic of Armenia, vol. 1 (1971).

nodes.label: Armenian–Azerbaijani clashes
nodes.full: In February 1905 street fighting between Armenians and Azerbaijanis in Baku, in a city of oil workers and rival economic and political grievances, spread to Nakhchivan, Erivan and Shusha, in the late summer, and in 1905–1906 caused thousands of deaths on both sides and the destruction of villages. Armenian and Azerbaijani accounts differ over the origins and the share of blame; the local authorities were accused of passivity or worse.
nodes.src: Tadeusz Swietochowski, Russian Azerbaijan (1985); Suny 1993; Altstadt 1992.

nodes.label: Gurian republic
nodes.full: In the Georgian province of Guria peasants and Social Democrats created in 1902–1906 a form of local self-rule, with their own courts, schools and militia, a 'Gurian republic', when the Russian state's authority collapsed; the Cossack punitive expeditions of 1906 brought the experiment to an end and executions.
nodes.src: Suny 1994; Eric Lohr and others on Guria.

nodes.label: Tbilisi bank robbery
nodes.full: On 26 June 1907 a band of Bolshevik militants led by Kamo (Simon Ter-Petrosian) held up an armoured cash coach in Yerevan Square in Tbilisi and escaped with about 340,000 roubles, leaving dozens killed or wounded; the money, intended for Lenin's party, was hard to change, and the affair was condemned by the Mensheviks. Stalin is believed to have taken part in planning it.
nodes.src: Police reports; Simon Sebag Montefiore, Young Stalin (2007).

nodes.label: Caucasus campaigns
nodes.full: The Russian Caucasus army under Vorontsov-Dashkov and then Yudenich defeated the Ottoman offensive at Sarıkamış in January 1915, took Van in 1915, Erzurum in February 1916 and Trebizond in April 1916, and held a large part of the Ottoman east until the collapse of the army in 1917; Armenian volunteer units were attached to the army.
nodes.src: William Allen and Paul Muratoff, Caucasian Battlefields (1953); Hovannisian 1971.

nodes.label: Georgian Legion
nodes.full: A group of Georgian émigrés and prisoners of war, working through a Georgian Committee in Berlin and with German and Ottoman support, formed a Georgian Legion in 1915–1916 in the hope of Georgian independence; it served on the Ottoman side and in the German army, and remained an episode in the complexity of Georgian politics.
nodes.src: Suny 1994; Georgian Committee records.

nodes.label: Armenian church property
nodes.full: By a law of 12 June 1903, the government placed the property of the Armenian church, its schools and funds, under the control of the Ministry of Interior, to end what it saw as a base of separatism; mass protests, closure of shops and violence followed, and the law was set aside in 1905.
nodes.src: Law of 12 June 1903; Suny 1993; Bournoutian, A Concise History of the Armenian People (2002).

nodes.label: Duma and the Caucasus
nodes.full: The Caucasus sent deputies to the four Russian Dumas; the first Duma of 1906 had Georgian Social Democrats under Nikolai Chkheidze and Irakli Tsereteli, Armenian and Azerbaijani deputies of liberal and national parties, while the electoral laws of 1907 greatly reduced the Caucasian representation, with Muslims and others losing seats.
nodes.src: Electoral law of 3 June 1907; Suny 1994; Swietochowski 1985.

nodes.label: Census of 1897
nodes.full: The first all-Russian census of 1897 counted about 9.3 million people in the Caucasus region, among them some 1.35 million Georgians, over a million Armenians and nearly 1.5 million 'Tatars' (Azerbaijanis) in Transcaucasia, by language and religion; it fixed the ethnic categories used by later politics.
nodes.src: First General Census of the Russian Empire (1897); Suny 1994.

nodes.label: Georgian autocephaly restored
nodes.full: On 12 March 1917, in the first days of the revolution, a congress of Georgian clergy and laymen at Mtskheta unilaterally restored the autocephaly of the Georgian church abolished in 1811, and in September Kirion Sadzaglishvili was elected Catholicos-Patriarch; the Russian Provisional Government did not recognise it.
nodes.src: Act of 12 March 1917; Rapp, Georgian Christian Identity (2003).

nodes.label: Jadidism
nodes.full: New-method (usul-i jadid) schools, with secular subjects in Azerbaijani and Russian, spread in the 1890s and 1900s, among them Zeynalabdin Taghiyev's schools in Baku and the Seyyid Azim Shirvani school; they trained a new class of teachers and writers. The conservative clergy opposed them, and in 1905–1907 Azerbaijanis demanded to set up their own school system.
nodes.src: Altstadt 1992; Swietochowski 1985.

nodes.label: Muslim congress
nodes.full: In April 1917 the first congress of the Muslims of the Caucasus was held in Baku with over 700 delegates, who discussed national autonomy, women's rights and education, and resolved to ask the new government for a federal Russian republic; it showed the strength of the Azerbaijani national movement.
nodes.src: Altstadt 1992; Swietochowski 1985.

nodes.label: Pirosmani
nodes.full: Niko Pirosmanishvili (1862–1918), a self-taught painter from Kakheti who painted shop signs and tavern pictures in Tbilisi, made an art of simplified, monumental images of the city's people, animals and feasts that were admired by Russian avant-garde artists, who discovered him in 1912, and which became emblematic of Georgian art; he died in poverty.
nodes.src: Pirosmani exhibition catalogues; Georgian National Museum.

nodes.label: Komitas and Hajibeyov
nodes.full: Komitas (1869–1935), trained in Berlin, collected and arranged Armenian folk songs and chants; Armen Tigranian's 'Anoush' (1912) became the national opera of Armenia; and Uzeyir Hajibeyov (1885–1948) staged the opera 'Leyli and Majnun' in Baku in 1908, the first opera in the Muslim world.
nodes.src: Komitas, Armenian Folk Songs; Tigranian, Anoush (1912); Hajibeyov, Leyli and Majnun (1908); Altstadt 1992.

nodes.label: Molla Nasreddin and the writers
nodes.full: The Armenian poet Hovhannes Tumanyan (1869–1923) wrote verse, tales and ballads of village life; the Georgian Vazha-Pshavela (1861–1915) wrote epics of the highlanders; and Jalil Mammadguluzadeh founded in Tbilisi in 1906 the satirical weekly 'Molla Nasreddin', which attacked clergy, landlords and imperial rule and was read from Tabriz to Istanbul. They mark the literary peak of the three nations.
nodes.src: Tumanyan, Poems; Vazha-Pshavela, Poems; Molla Nasreddin (1906–1931); Swietochowski 1985.

nodes.label: Baku mansions
nodes.full: The oil magnates, Taghiyev, Mantashev, Nagiyev and Asadullayev, built in Baku mansions in Gothic, Venetian and Moorish style, such as Taghiyev's house (1895–1901) and Ismailiyya (1913), along with the theatre of 1911, so that the city became a showpiece of European and Oriental styles.
nodes.src: Altstadt 1992; Baku architectural surveys.

nodes.label: Dashnaks
nodes.full: The Armenian Revolutionary Federation (Dashnaktsutyun), founded in Tbilisi in 1890, combined nationalism and socialism and organised armed bands for the Armenians of the Ottoman Empire, and in Russia supported the defence of the church in 1903 and then fought in the 1905 clashes; it became the dominant party of Russian Armenians.
nodes.src: Louise Nalbandian, The Armenian Revolutionary Movement (1963); Suny 1993.

nodes.label: Mesame Dasi and Mensheviks
nodes.full: The Georgian Social Democrats, the 'Third Group' (Mesame Dasi) of Noe Zhordania, formed in 1892, became after 1903 the Menshevik wing of the Russian Social Democratic Party, with a base in the peasants of Guria and workers of Tbilisi and Chiatura; they dominated Georgian politics from 1905 and led the independence movement.
nodes.src: Noe Zhordania, My Life (1968); Suny 1994.

nodes.label: Hummet and Musavat
nodes.full: The Muslim Social Democratic Hummet ('Energy') group, founded in Baku in 1904 by Narimanov and others, appealed to the oil workers; the Musavat ('Equality') party, founded in 1911 by Mammad Amin Rasulzade, was the main Azerbaijani nationalist party, and the writers of the journal Füyuzat (1906–1907) under Ali bey Huseynzade put forward the programme of becoming Turkic, Islamic and modern.
nodes.src: Swietochowski 1985; Altstadt 1992.

nodes.label: Stalin on the national question
nodes.full: Ioseb Jughashvili (Stalin), from Gori in Georgia, a former seminarian who had been active in Tbilisi and Baku revolutionary circles, wrote in Vienna in 1913 the essay 'Marxism and the National Question', which defined a nation by language, territory, economic life and psychological make-up, and which became the basis of Soviet nationality policy.
nodes.src: J. V. Stalin, Marxism and the National Question (1913); Montefiore 2007.

nodes.label: Baku oil
nodes.full: Baku's output grew from some 400,000 tonnes in 1880 to 11 million in 1901, about half of the world's oil, as the Nobel brothers' Branobel, the Rothschilds' Caspian and Black Sea company and many smaller firms, including Armenian and Muslim magnates, drilled and refined; the oil workers' population and the cost to health and environment grew in step.
nodes.src: Altstadt 1992; Suny 1994; Fuad Aliyev on Baku oil.

nodes.label: Manganese, copper, cognac
nodes.full: The manganese mines of Chiatura in Georgia, opened in 1879, supplied about half of the world's manganese by 1900; the copper smelters of Alaverdi and Zangezur were developed in the 1890s and 1900s, and in Yerevan the cognac works of Tairov (1887) and Shustov (1899) were founded. Georgian tea at Chakva (1893) and tobacco spread.
nodes.src: Suny 1994; Suny 1993.

nodes.label: Village after emancipation
nodes.full: The Caucasian peasants had to pay redemption dues to their lords, and land shortage and debt were pressing in Georgia, Imereti and Karabakh; many left to work in Baku's oilfields, the mines and Tbilisi's factories, and the nobility's share fell, as merchants and townsmen bought land.
nodes.src: Suny 1994; Altstadt 1992.

nodes.label: Surami tunnel and pipeline
nodes.full: The Transcaucasian railway was completed from Poti and Batum to Tbilisi and Baku in 1883, with the great Surami (Likhi) tunnel of 1890 eliminating the steep pass; a kerosene pipeline from Baku to Batum, some 835 kilometres, was built in 1906–1907 to bring oil to the Black Sea. Batum became a major oil port.
nodes.src: Railway statutes; Altstadt 1992; Suny 1994.

nodes.label: Trams, funicular, films
nodes.full: Tbilisi had a horse tram from 1883, electric trams from 1904 and a funicular up Mtatsminda from 1905; films were first shown in Tbilisi in 1896 and in Baku in 1898, when Aleksandr Mishon filmed the Sabunchu oil fountain, the first film made in Azerbaijan.
nodes.src: Municipal histories of Tbilisi and Baku.

nodes.label: Nobels and Rothschilds
nodes.full: Foreign capital shaped Baku: the Nobel brothers' company (Branobel, 1879) built tankers and pipelines, the Rothschilds financed the Batum railway and refineries from 1883, and the world market changed the city; Branobel's director Ludwig Nobel and his sons made Baku a centre of Swedish industry.
nodes.src: Robert Tolf, The Russian Rockefellers (1976); Altstadt 1992.

nodes.label: Refugees of 1915
nodes.full: In 1915 the massacres and deportations of Armenians in the Ottoman Empire and the Russian advance sent several hundred thousand Armenian refugees from Van, Bitlis and Erzurum across the border into Russian Armenia, where they were housed and fed by Armenian relief bodies, Russian and western charities and the Etchmiadzin catholicosate, in a famine and typhus. Many Muslim villagers had also fled the front.
nodes.src: Hovannisian 1971; Peter Balakian, The Burning Tigris (2003); Altstadt 1992.

nodes.label: Shamakhi earthquake and 1905 fires
nodes.full: A major earthquake destroyed much of Shamakhi on 13 February 1902, killing thousands and shifting the provincial centre; in the troubles of September 1905 many of Baku's oil derricks and plants were set on fire in an arson campaign and burned for days, an event that ended production for a time and brought the international price of oil up.
nodes.src: Altstadt 1992; Suny 1994.

nodes.label: First collective agreement
nodes.full: In December 1904 a strike of the oil workers in Baku, organised by the Social Democrats, led to the first collective labour agreement in Russia, with shorter hours, higher pay and the recognition of workers' representatives; the workers, Azerbaijani, Persian, Armenian, Russian and Georgian, were housed in barracks and lived in poor conditions.
nodes.src: Altstadt 1992; Suny 1994.

nodes.label: School for Muslim girls
nodes.full: The oil magnate Zeynalabdin Taghiyev founded in 1901 in Baku the first secular school for Muslim girls in the Caucasus, with the support of the educator Hasan bey Zardabi, in the face of opposition by clergy; by 1917 Azerbaijani women were taking part in public life and a Muslim women's congress was held in Baku that year.
nodes.src: Altstadt 1992; Swietochowski 1985.

nodes.label: Refugees at Etchmiadzin
nodes.full: Relief workers' reports describe refugees camped in the open at Etchmiadzin and Yerevan, orphans and the sick, dying in hundreds from typhus, hunger and cold; the catholicosate's orphanages and the American and Russian committees fed and sheltered many thousands.
nodes.src: Relief committee reports (1915–1917); Hovannisian 1971.

nodes.label: Berlin and the new borders
nodes.full: At the Congress of Berlin in 1878 the Ottomans ceded Kars, Ardahan and Batum to Russia, which organised Kars as an oblast and Batum as a free port.
